title: Stations Built in Pieces
question: How did space stations go from one-piece labs to stations joined together from parts?
hook: The first stations went up whole and were left behind once the supplies ran out.
idea: Docking ports let later stations receive visiting crews and supply craft, and a docking test on Salyut 7 pointed toward modular stations.

beats.prompt: put these docking firsts in order, earliest first
items: First space rendezvous without docking (Gemini 6 and 7)

beats.prompt: sort each description into the kind of station it fits
items: Held all its supplies from launch
Abandoned after the supplies ran out
Could host a second visiting crew
beats.explain: Early stations were launched whole with their supplies and left behind, while the second port on Salyut 6 and 7 allowed second crews and Progress supplies.

beats.prompt: one step in this reasoning is wrong; which?
steps: Early stations were launched in one piece with all their supplies.
Once those supplies were used up, the station was abandoned.
So adding a second docking port could not help a station last longer.
Salyut 6 and 7 had a second port that let a second crew and Progress supplies arrive.
beats.explain: The second port let visiting crews and supply craft arrive, which let a crew man the station continually.

beats.prompt: A station is built in orbit from separate pieces. Which feature lets a new module join it?

choices.label: Station-keeping thrusters
choices.feedback: Thrusters help the station stay in place; they are not how modules join it.

choices.label: A rotating wheel
choices.feedback: A rotating wheel was a concept for artificial gravity, and development of one was never begun in the 20th century.

choices.label: Research laboratories
choices.feedback: Laboratories are where experiments happen, not how modules are joined.

beats.explain: Modular stations are built and maintained through docking ports, which allow modules to be joined or moved.
